Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”.

contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it 
is bereft of valid support and devoid of merit.

engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So

she was appointed as an Assistant by the 2™ Partyin a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 07.09.20] by

regularization of her services for the services rendered by her and that she was doing the duties of regular staff; that

deprived with the benefits of the permanent employees; that she was not provided with Provident Fund, Bonus 
Benefits though other employees were extended with the same; that she was suddenly retrenched from the services 
of the II Party orally from 8.2.207 in the morning hours by the Branch Manager without notice, without payment 
of notice pay/ retrenchment compensation though there were no allegations against her.She was retrenched from the 
services without prior intimation or paying her retrenchment compensation and without following due process of law 
and that the II Party has retrenched more than 20 workmen without filing approval application seeking permission 
from the appropriate Government to retrench their services as mandated under Section 25N of the Act; that due to

work done by her is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal and malafide;that she raised an

declare the retrenchment of service by the II Party as not in accordance with the provisions of ID Act; reinstate her 
into service with full backwages and other benefits, regularization with continuity of service and ancillary benefits 
from the date of her appointment 07.09.20 l with cost. 

2. The 2" Party in their Counter Statement rebutted the Claim Statement stating that all the averments made are 
false; that LIC of India (Staff) Regulations, 960 are not applicable to the temporary employees appointed by the II 
Party; that the I Party is put to strict proof of the above averments; that she was doing some unspecified job on daily 
wages on need basis and that they were paying wages as per the notification issued by the Government of Karnataka 
from time to time and therefore the question of extending Provident Fund Benefits does not arise. As the specified 
job was completed, her services were disengaged as per law and the question of issuing notice, retrenchment 
compensation or notice pay does not arise and that the II Party has not contravened the provisions of ID Act and the 
question of reinstatement with the backwages and other benefits does not arise. The Respondent has prayed for 
dismissal of the Petition with cost. 


3. On the rival pleadings the following pointsarise for consideration: 


“0i. Whether the I Party has succeeded in proving that she was appointed by the II Party as Assistant 
on temporary basis in a clear vacancy as contended? 

02. Whether the disengagement of the I Party from job by the II Party is illegal as contended by the I

04. What is the proper order to be passed?”

7. The I Party WW I claimed herself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear 
vacancy of Office Assistant under the II Party LIC of India since 07.09.20] lat its ChitradurgaBranch and continued 
to work for Six years till l8.2.20l7. Her case is that she has put in an application before the II Party and she was 
interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to her she was appointed with an assurance

of regularization of her service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent Assistants. The 
above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the II Party on the precincts that the I Party was engaged by the LIC 
purely on daily wages to perform some unspecified jobs and she has been paid daily wage for the days of her 
engagement. Such payment according to the II Party has never been meant as “SALARY”. 


8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW |, there is nothing indicting her to have been called for 
an interview for the post of Office Assistant. She did not produce copy of application said to have been submitted by 
her before the II Party to the said post. Though she claimed that the II Party did publish notification calling for 
applications on their notice board, she could not specify the date of notification or its exhibition on the notice board. 
She was not issued with any appointment letter by the IT Party. On meticulous cross-examination she testified that she 
was appointed on temporary basis as daily wager. She was given wages for the period she served in the II Party. Ex 
W-I series are the Seven vouchers produced by the I Party to prove the payments received by her from the II Party 
LIC. The vouchers reflect the wages received by the I Party and similarly placed other workers. Those vouchers 
would never improve her case, much less it substantiates her contention that she was appointed in a clear vacancy by 
undergoing regular recruitment process. Those vouchers would never indicate continuous and uninterrupted service 
of the I Party under the II Party for Six years as contended by her. 


9. MW | हल Divisional Manager of the II Party specifically deposed that there is no particular notification for 
LIC separately for daily wage employees and such daily wagers were engaged based on need and requirements and 
there is no prescribed recruitment procedure for engaging them. Their wages were paid monthly in cash, debited from 
imprest Cash Account No. !772. This fact stood revealed from Ex ५४-] series vouchers. MW | reiterated that no 
order is issued to such persons for engaging them on daily wage. So without getting an appointment order from the 
management the I Party worker cannot qualify for herself to be entitled for permanency or rather regularization in the 
job. There is no basis for the so called assurance alleged to have been given by the II Party that she would be given 
permanency in service along with equivalent other benefits. 


0. The purpose of production of Ex W-2 by the I Party, the confidential communication issued by the Regional 
Manager (P&IR) to all SDM under South Central Zones dated 25..207 alerting the divisions to disengage all the 
daily wagers who are continued without any court case and calling for the number of daily wagers continuing by 
virtue of court cases pursuant to the decision of the competent authority is not profitably explained by the I Party. It 
is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody of Ex W-2, the confidential 
communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex W-2 is not of any help to the I Party to establish 
her case. 


Il. Ex W-3dated 25.2.20I7 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager seeking 
regularization of her service being aggrieved by stoppage of her service w.e.f. l8.2.20l7stating the same as 
retrenchment. In Ex W-3 she grieved before the authority that she was pulled out from job without notice and 
without payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despitehaving no allegations against her. 


2. On 27.2.20!7 she took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), Hubli 
under Ex W-4. Ex W-5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the Ex W-4 
representation. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager 
on need basis due to office exigencies and she was neither recruited not given any appointment letter by any 
authority. Her engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on peace meal basis depending upon the 
needs of the office and not as a temporary employee. Her pay of wages was as per the Government of Karnataka 
Gazette Notification revised from time to time. MW | during her evidence precisely testified that since the I Party 
was paid wages counting the number of days she worked, no deduction was made from her wage towards Provident 
Fund and payment of bonus to her also did not arise for consideration. The circumstances explained by MW [ 
substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager without there 
being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance being out of place. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.208 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application filed 
by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. Ex W-0 is the copy of notification to the post of Recruitment of Assistant 
published by the II Party on 7.09.209. She did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. She 
testified that she is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-] is the representation given by the I Party 
to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one post of 
Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point of 
controversy as to the status of employment at the time of her engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been an 
engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement

of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District Judge, 
Mirzapur and another 200l | SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana 
vs. Jasmer Singh (996 () SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot 
be treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar 
posts. Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for 
regular workers, nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of 
recruitment. They are not selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In 
other words the requirements for selection are not as rigorous. There are also other 
provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of the service to be 
transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be 
equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the 
minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 
Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State ofHaryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he holds 
no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she performed under 
the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was engaged by the II 
Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I Party was for meeting 
the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work performed is thus well 
founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held to 
be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in the 
procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial recruitment 
and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the all-important 
condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made against the 
Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC I) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the instant case the I party 
is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “/ong duration of work” (emphasis 
supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of valid 
support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her engagement 
was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 0.02.2025 
awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two decades of service 
he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down by the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual Employment terminates 


5724 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been engaged beyond the 
period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made permanent, if the 
original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal position settled at 
rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, regularization, 
continuity of service or backwages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-l vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective 
years and there is no valid material proving that her engagement was continuous in nature and she performed duties 
under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time 
was more than 240 days in a calendar year and her disengagement was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F 
of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the 
relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually her Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be 
dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered accordingly. 


2I. POINT NO. 4:In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

an engagement as Daily Wager, she does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party

Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of her service and she has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which she claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37.

Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (Il) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State ofHaryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in her pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works she 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by her as to the nature of the duties for which she was 
engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I 
Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work 
performed is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 
the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”.

discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats her claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit.

the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process.

decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual

Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or backwages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-! vouchers show only pay for a single month in the respective

under the II Party continuously till the date of her disengagement so as to show that her tenure of service at a time

Ls This is a Petition filed under Section 2A of the ID act. The claim set forth by the |7 party workman is that 


he was appointed as an Assistant by the 27 Party in a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 5.05.202 by 
obtaining an Application and he has attended the interview conducted by the II Party; he was also assured with 
regularization of his services for the services rendered by him and that he was doing the duties of regular staff; that 
he was not paid with minimum scales as applicable to the Assistants and took work for more than eight hours per 
day without paying him overtime wages; inspite of repeated requests to absorb him to the permanent post he was 
deprived with the benefits of the permanent employees; that he was not provided with Provident Fund, Bonus 
Benefits though other employees were extended with the same; that he was suddenly retrenched from the services 
of the II Party orally from 8.2.20!7 in the morning hours by the Branch Manager without notice, without 
payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation though there were no allegations against him. He was 
retrenched from the services without prior intimation or paying him retrenchment compensation and without 
following due process of law and that the II Party has retrenched more than 20 workmen without filing approval 
application seeking permission from the appropriate Government to retrench their services as mandated under 
Section 25N of the Act; that due to the retrenchment he is facing irreparable hardship, agony and unable to run his 
family and that he does not know any other work than the Assistant job; that the II Party has employed fresh 
entrants in his place and the nature of work done by him is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal 
and malafide; that he raised an industrial dispute since no settlement was arrived he preferred to file the present 
petition requesting this Tribunal to declare the retrenchment of service by the II Party as not in accordance with the 
provisions of ID Act; reinstate him into service with full back wages and other benefits, regularization with 
continuity of service and ancillary benefits from the date of his appointment 5.05.202 with cost. 


2. The 2™ Party in their Counter Statement rebutted the Claim Statement stating that all the averments made 
are false; that LIC of India (Staff) Regulations, !960 are not applicable to the temporary employees appointed by 
the II Party; that the I Party is put to strict proof of the above averments; that he was doing some unspecified job on 
daily wages on need basis and that they were paying wages as per the notification issued by the Government of 
Karnataka from time to time and therefore the question of extending Provident Fund Benefits does not arise. As 
the specified job was completed, his services were disengaged as per law and the question of issuing notice, 
retrenchment compensation or notice pay does not arise and that the II Party has not contravened the provisions of 
ID Act and the question of reinstatement with the backwages and other benefits does not arise. The Respondent 
has prayed for dismissal of the Petition with cost. 


3. On the rival pleadings the following points arise for consideration: 


“0i. Whether the I Party has succeeded in proving that he was appointed by the II Party as 
Assistant on temporary basis in a clear vacancy as contended? 


02. Whether the disengagement of the I Party from job by the II Party is illegal as contended 
by the I Party? 


03. Whether the I Party is entitled for the reliefs prayed for? 
04. What is the proper order to be passed?”

sides.

and interwoven, all these points are discussed together.

7 The I Party WW | claimed himself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear 
vacancy of Office Assistant under the II Party LIC of India since 5.05.202 at its Holalkere Satellite Branch and 
continued to work for Five years till 8.l2.20I7. His case is that he has put in an application before the II Party 
and he was interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to him he was appointed with 
an assurance of regularization of his service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent 
Assistants. The above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the IJ Party on the precincts that the I Party was 
engaged by the LIC purely on daily wages to perform some unspecified jobs and he has been paid daily wage for 
the days of his engagement. Such payment according to the II Party has never been meant as “SALARY”. 


8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW l|, there is nothing indicting him to have been called 
for an interview for the post of Office Assistant. He did not produce copy of application said to have been 
submitted by him before the II Party to the said post. Though he claimed that the II Party did publish notification 
calling for applications on their notice board, he could not specify the date of notification or its exhibition on the 
notice board. He was not issued with any appointment letter by the II Party. On meticulous cross-examination he 
testified that he was appointed on temporary basis as daily wager. He was given wages for the period he served in 
the II Party. Ex ४४-] series are three vouchers produced by the I Party to prove the payments received by him from 
the II Party LIC. The vouchers reflect the wages received by the I Party and similarly placed other workers. Those 
vouchers would never improve his case, much less it substantiates his contention that he was appointed in a clear 
vacancy by undergoing regular recruitment process. Those vouchers would never indicate continuous and 
uninterrupted service of the I Party under the II Party for Five years as contended by him. 


9. MW | the Divisional Manager of the वा Party specifically deposed that there is no particular notification 
for LIC separately for daily wage employees and such daily wagers were engaged based on need and requirements 
and there is no prescribed recruitment procedure for engaging them. Their wages were paid monthly in cash, 
debited from imprest Cash Account No. l772. This fact stood revealed from Ex ४४-] series vouchers. MW | 
reiterated that no order is issued to such persons for engaging them on daily wage. So without getting an 
appointment order from the management the I Party worker cannot qualify for himself to be entitled for 
permanency or rather regularization in the job. There is no basis for the so called assurance alleged to have been 
given by the II Party that he would be given permanency in service along with equivalent other benefits. 


0. The purpose of production of Ex W-2 by the I Party, the confidential communication issued by the 
Regional Manager (P&IR) to all SDM under South Central Zones dated 25..207 alerting the divisions to 
disengage all the daily wagers who are continued without any court case and calling for the number of daily 
wagers continuing by virtue of court cases pursuant to the decision of the competent authority is not profitably 
explained by the I Party. It is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody 
of Ex W-2, the confidential communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex ४४-२2 is not of any 
help to the I Party to establish his case. 


Il. Ex W-3 dated 25.2.207 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager 
seeking regularization of his service being aggrieved by stoppage of his service w.e.f. |8.2.207 stating the same 
as retrenchment. In Ex W-3 he grieved before the authority that he was pulled out from job without notice and 
without payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despite having no allegations against him. 


2. On 5.2.20i8 he took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), 
Hubli under Ex W-4. Ex W-5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, purported to be in 
response to Ex W-4 representation. Ex W-7 is shown to be the Joint discussion conducted by the Assistant Labour 
Commissioner(C) in the matter on 05.02.208. However, the conciliation failure report produced by the I Party 
issued by the ALC(C) would demonstrate that the conciliation was commenced from 08.0.208, seemingly much 
prior to the Application submitted by the I Party. In short there are altogether obvious mismatching of dates in the 
respective documents produced by the I Party. Anyhow, the ultimate fact emerging is that the Conciliation attempt 
was ended in failure which caused the I Party to approach this Court seeking redressal of his grievance. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. Ex W-8 is also a similar application filed by the I Party before the 
Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the conciliation proceedings. Ex 
W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of documents from various branches. 
During cross-examination WW | testified the II Party has called for application for Assistant Post and he is not 
eligible to file application to the said post. 


4. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager on 
need basis due to office exigencies and he was neither recruited not given any appointment letter by any authority. 
His engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on peace meal basis depending upon the needs of 
the office and not as a temporary employee. His pay of wages was as per the Government of Karnataka Gazette 
Notification revised from time to time. MW | during his evidence precisely testified that since the I Party was 
paid wages counting the number of days he worked, no deduction was made from his wage towards Provident 
Fund and payment of bonus to him also did not arise for consideration. The circumstances explained by MW |

substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager without there 
being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance being out of place. 


5. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of his engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, he does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further 
requirement of his service and he has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits 
sought for, relied upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be 
observed that the I Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis 
of which he claims reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In 
order to high light the said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and 
others vs. District Judge, Mirzapur and another 200 SCC 37. 


6. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 () SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be 
treated as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. 
Daily-rated workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, 
nor do they have to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not 
selected in the manner in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for 
selection are not as rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the 
liability of a member of the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary 
jurisdiction of the authorities as prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. 
They cannot, therefore, be equated with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can 
they claim the minimum of the regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in his pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works he 
performed under the II Party, much less any material is placed by him as to the nature of the duties for which he 
was engaged by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the 
I Party was for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the 
work performed is thus well founded. 


7. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to 
do so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is 
held to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some 
flaws in the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


8. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 
(4) SCC ) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the 
contract, if it were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end 
when it is discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of 
his term of appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage 
worker is continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in 
regular service or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was 
not made by following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to 
prevent regular recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an 
end or of ad hoc employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.” Here in the 
instant case the I party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “Jong duration 
of work” (emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats his claim as it is 
bereft of valid support and devoid of merit. 


9. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners 
therein were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from

shortlisted candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor 
her engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


20. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or 
made permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So 
the legal position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of 
reinstatement, regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


2]. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex १४-। seires indicate the payment made to the I Party in the year 
205 alone for the month of March and November and there is no valid material proving that his engagement was 
continuous in nature and hhe performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of his disengagement so 
as to show that his tenure of service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and his disengagement 
was in violation of the provisions of Section 25F of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I 
Party failed to establish a case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually 
his Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered 
accordingly. 


22. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief. 
23. In the result, the following Award is passed 
AWARD 
The Claim Petition is Dismissed. No order as to cost.

valid support and devoid of merit.

l. This is a Petition filed under Section 2A of the ID act. The claim set forth by the |“ party workman is that 


he was appointed as an Assistant by the 2™ Party in a clear vacancy of Office Assistant w.e.f. 02.04.20I2 by

the services without prior intimation or paying him retrenchment compensation and without following due process

that due to the retrenchment he is facing irreparable hardship, agony and unable to run his family and that he does 
not know any other work than the Assistant job; that the II Party has employed fresh entrants in his place and the 
nature of work done by him is perennial in nature and taking the new entrants is illegal and malafide; that he raised 
an industrial dispute since no settlement was arrived he preferred to file the present petition requesting this Tribunal 
to declare the retrenchment of service by the II Party as not in accordance with the provisions of ID Act; reinstate

benefits from the date of his appointment 02.04.202 with cost. 


2. The 2™ Party in their Counter Statement rebutted the Claim Statement stating that all the averments made 
are false; that LIC of India (Staff) Regulations, 960 are not applicable to the temporary employees appointed by the 
II Party; that the I Party is put to strict proof of the above averments; that he was doing some unspecified job on

retrenchment compensation or notice pay does not arise and that the II Party has not contravened the provisions of

3. On the rival pleadings the following points arise for consideration: 


“0i. Whether the I Party has succeeded in proving that he was appointed by the II Party as Assistant 
on temporary basis in a clear vacancy as contended? 


02. Whether the disengagement of the I Party from job by the II Party is illegal as contended by the I 
Party? 


03. Whether the I Party is entitled for the reliefs prayed for? 
04. What is the proper order to be passed?”

the II Party MW | is examined and Ex ॥-] is marked. 

5. Heard the arguments advanced by both sides. Written notes of Arguments are also submitted by both sides. 
6. POINTS NO. TO 3: Since the matter to be considered and adjudicated on these points are intertwined 


and interwoven, all these points are discussed together. 


7. The I Party WW | claimed himself as a temporary employee / Assistant in Class III Category in a clear 
vacancy of Office Assistant under the II Party LIC of India since 02.04.202 at its Harihara Branch and continued to 
work for Six years till 6.2.20l7. His case is that he has put in an application before the II Party and he was 
interviewed by the officials of the LIC at the Branch Office. According to him he was appointed with an assurance 
of regularization of his service within a few years coupled with the benefits applicable to permanent Assistants. The 
above claim of the I Party is stoutly denied by the II Party on the precincts that the I Party was engaged by the LIC 
purely on daily wages to perform some unspecified jobs and he has been paid daily wage for the days of his 
engagement. Such payment according to the II Party has never been meant as “SALARY”. 


8. Among the documents produced and proved by WW |, there is nothing indicting him to have been called 
for an interview for the post of Office Assistant. He did not produce copy of application said to have been submitted 
by him before the II Party to the said post. Though he claimed that the II Party did publish notification calling for 
applications on their notice board, he could not specify the date of notification or its exhibition on the notice board. 
He was not issued with any appointment letter by the II Party. On meticulous cross-examination he testified that he 
was appointed on temporary basis as daily wager. He was given wages for the period he served in the II Party. Ex 
W-I series are five vouchers produced by the I Party to prove the payments received by him from the II Party LIC. 
The vouchers reflect the wages received by the I Party and similarly placed other workers. Those vouchers would 
never improve his case, much less it substantiates his contention that he was appointed in a clear vacancy by 
undergoing regular recruitment process. Those vouchers would never indicate continuous and uninterrupted service 
of the I Party under the II Party for Six years as contended by him. 


9. MW | the Divisional Manager of the II Party specifically deposed that there is no particular notification for 
LIC separately for daily wage employees and such daily wagers were engaged based on need and requirements and 
there is no prescribed recruitment procedure for engaging them. Their wages were paid monthly in cash, debited 
from imprest Cash Account No. !!772. This fact stood revealed from Ex W-I series vouchers. MW I reiterated 
that no order is issued to such persons for engaging them on daily wage. So without getting an appointment order 
from the management the I Party worker cannot qualify for himself to be entitled for permanency or rather 
regularization in the job. There is no basis for the so called assurance alleged to have been given by the II Party that 
he would be given permanency in service along with equivalent other benefits. 


0. The purpose of production of Ex W-2 by the I Party, the confidential communication issued by the 
Regional Manager (P&IR) to all SDM under South Central Zones dated 25.i.20i7 alerting the divisions to 
disengage all the daily wagers who are continued without any court case and calling for the number of daily wagers 
continuing by virtue of court cases pursuant to the decision of the competent authority is not profitably explained by 
the I Party. It is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody of Ex W-2, the

confidential communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex W-2 is not of any help to the I 
Party to establish his case. 


Il. Ex W-3 dated 25.2.20l7 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager 
seeking regularization of his service being aggrieved by stoppage of his service w.e.f. l8.2.207 stating the same as 
retrenchment. In Ex W-3 he grieved before the authority that he was pulled out from job without notice and without 
payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despite having no allegations against him. 


2. On 27.2.207 he took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), Hubli 
under Ex W-4. Ex W-S5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the Ex W-4 
representation. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager 
on need basis due to office exigencies and he was neither recruited not given any appointment letter by any 
authority. His engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on peace meal basis depending upon 
the needs of the office and not as a temporary employee. His pay of wages was as per the Government of Karnataka 
Gazette Notification revised from time to time. MW | during his evidence precisely testified that since the I Party 
was paid wages counting the number of days he worked, no deduction was made from his wage towards Provident 
Fund and payment of bonus to him also did not arise for consideration. The circumstances explained by MW | 
substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager without there 
being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance being out of place. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.20I8 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application 
filed by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. Ex W-I0 is the copy of notification to the post of Recruitment of Assistant 
published by the I Party on 7.09.209. He did not prefer to put in an Application against such notification. He 
testified that he is not eligible to file application to the said post. Ex W-I] is the representation given by the I Party 
to the Chairman, LIC of India requesting to appoint her to the vacancy notified and if not, to keep vacant one post of 
Office Assistant till the instant case gets over. 


None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point of 
controversy as to the status of employment at the time of his engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been an 
engagement as Daily Wager, he does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The I Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of his service and he has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which he claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


5. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (Il) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in his pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works he performed 
under the II Party, much less any material is placed by him as to the nature of the duties for which he was engaged 
by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I Party was 
for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work performed 
is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 


5748 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 
the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 


against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ]) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work” 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats his claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 


20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-| seires indicate the payment made to the I Party in the year 
205 alone for the month of March and November and there is no valid material proving that his engagement was 
continuous in nature and hhe performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of his disengagement so 
as to show that his tenure of service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and his disengagement was 
in violation of the provisions of Section 25F of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party 
failed to establish a case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually his 
Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered 
accordingly. 


2I. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief.

The Claim Petition is Dismissed. No order as to cost.

the I Party. It is also not properly explained as to how the I Party / WW | happened to be in custody of Ex W-2, the 
confidential communication addressed to the SDM by its higher-up. Anyhow Ex W-2 is not of any help to the I 
Party to establish his case. 


Il. Ex W-3 dated 25.2.20l7 is the representation made by the I Party to the Senior Divisional Manager 
seeking reinstatement and regularization of his service being aggrieved by stoppage of his service w.e.f. 8.2.207 
stating the same as retrenchment. In Ex W-3 he grieved before the authority that he was pulled out from job without 
notice and without payment of notice pay / retrenchment compensation despite having no allegations against him. 


2. On 27.2.207 he took up the matter for conciliation before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), Hubli 
under Ex W-4. Ex W-S5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the Ex W-4 
representation. Ex W-5 is the reply submitted by the II Party before the ALC(C), Hubli, in response to the Ex W-4 
representation. All along, the II Party has adopted a firm defence that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager 
on need basis due to office exigencies and he was neither recruited not given any appointment letter by any 
authority. His engagement was purely on daily wages for carrying out work on peace meal basis depending upon 
the needs of the office and not as a temporary employee. His pay of wages was as per the Government of Karnataka 
Gazette Notification revised from time to time. MW | during his evidence precisely testified that since the I Party 
was paid wages counting the number of days he worked, no deduction was made from his wage towards Provident 
Fund and payment of bonus to him also did not arise for consideration. The circumstances explained by MW | 
substantiates the contention raised by the II Party that the I Party was engaged only as a daily wager without there 
being any assurance of permanency of service and such alleged assurance being out of place. 


3. Ex W-6 is the application filed by the I Party before the ALC(C) calling for documents from the II party 
during the conciliation proceedings. As per Ex W-7 the Assistant Labour Commissioner(C) conducted Joint 
Discussion on 05.02.20I8 notifying further joint discussion to another date. Ex W-8 is also a similar application 
filed by the I Party before the Conciliation Officer calling for some more documents from the II party during the 
conciliation proceedings. Ex W-9 is the letter issued by the ALC(C) to LEO for collection of photocopies of 
documents from various branches. He testified he had applied for the said post and he is not aware as to what 
developed there on. 


4. None of the above documents produced and relied upon by the I Party renders any proof to the core point 
of controversy as to the status of employment at the time of his engagement under the II Party. Indeed, had it been 
an engagement as Daily Wager, he does not get entitled for any of the benefits sought in the Petition. The II Party 
Management to buttress its contention that the I Party was simply disengaged as there existed no further requirement 
of his service and he has not been a temporary employee capable of claiming any of the benefits sought for, relied 
upon various judicial pronouncements of the Hon’ble Apex Court. At the threshold it has to be observed that the I 
Party failed in showing any Rule, Law or Regulation nor any administrative order on the basis of which he claims 
reinstatement and regularization with continuity of Service and other monetory benefits. In order to high light the 
said aspect the II Party has relied upon the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Subedar Singh and others vs. District 
Judge, Mirzapur and another 200I SCC 37. 


45. It is contextually significant to follow the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of 
Haryana vs. Jasmer Singh (996 (Il) SCC 77) which reads : 


“The respondents, therefore in the present appeals who are employed on daily wages cannot be treated 
as on a par with persons in regular service of the State of Haryana holding similar posts. Daily-rated 
workers are not required to possess the qualifications prescribed for regular workers, nor do they have 
to fulfil the requirement relating to age at the time of recruitment. They are not selected in the manner 
in which regular employees are selected. In other words the requirements for selection are not as 
rigorous. There are also other provisions relating to regular service such as the liability of a member of 
the service to be transferred, and his being subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the authorities as 
prescribed, which the daily-rated workmen are not subjected to. They cannot, therefore, be equated 
with regular workmen for the purposes for their wages. Nor can they claim the minimum of the 
regular pay-scale of the regularly employed” 


5752 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Referring to the said legal position the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Haryana and another vs. Tilak Raj and 
others (2003 (6) SCC 23) held that a scale of pay is attached to a definite post and in case of a daily wager, he 
holds no posts. The I Party neither in his pleadings nor in evidence has made out the particular works he performed 
under the II Party, much less any material is placed by him as to the nature of the duties for which he was engaged 
by the II Party. The contention of the II Party in its Statement of Objection that the engagement of the I Party was 
for meeting the office exigencies to attend some unspecified jobs on payment of daily wage for the work performed 
is thus well founded. 


6. In Mohammed Ashif and others vs. State of Bihar and others (200 (5) SCC 475), the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court held that the question of regularization of services of an Employee may arise only in situations where against 
an available clear vacancy an appointment is made on adhoc or on-daily wage basis by an authority competent to do 
so without any artificial break in service. The second situation in which the regularization could be granted is held 
to be where the initial entry of the employee against an available vacancy was found suffering from some flaws in 
the procedure in making the appointment though the person appointing was competent to make such initial 
recruitment and had otherwise followed the procedure prescribed for such recruitment. It is equally held that “the 
all-important condition precedent for such regularization is that the initial entry of such employee must be made 
against the Sanctioned vacancy and by following the Rules and Regulations governing such entry”. 


7. Similarly the constitution bench of the Hon’ble Apex Court in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi (2006 (4) 
SCC ]) held that “Jf it is a contractual appointment, the appointment comes to an end at the end of the contract, if it 
were an engagement or appointment on daily wages or casual basis, the same would come to an end when it is 
discontinued. Similarly, a temporary employee could not claim to be made permanent on the expiry of his term of 
appointment. It has also to be clarified that merely because a temporary employee or a casual wage worker is 
continued for a time beyond the term of his appointment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed in regular service 
or made permanent, merely on the strength of such continuance, if the original appointment was not made by 
following a due process of selection as envisaged by the relevant rules. It is not open to the court to prevent regular 
recruitment at the instance of temporary employees whose period of employment has come to an end or of ad hoc 
employees who by the very nature of their appointment, do not acquire any right.’ Here in the instant case the I 
party is claiming permanency and seeks for regularization mainly on the so called “long duration of work’ 
(emphasis supplied) and not on any other valid ground. The dictum quoted above defeats his claim as it is bereft of 
valid support and devoid of merit. 


8. Most of the rulings placed by the I party are not applicable to the facts of the case on hand. The Verdict of 
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras in V Muthukumarasamy and others vs. The Chairman, LIC, Zonal Office 
dated 2.0.2007 also does not get any application in view of the fact involved in that case as the Petitioners therein 
were sponsored by the Employment Exchange and have been appointed on temporary basis from shortlisted 
candidates. As already observed, the I Party herein was not sponsored by Employment Exchange nor her 
engagement was in a clear vacancy by undergoing the Regular Recruitment process. 


9. The I party further relied upon on the ruling of the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, Bengaluru in R V 
Mohan Reddy vs. The Chairman, Karnataka Grameena Bank in WP No. 944/2022 (L-RES) dated 
0.02.2025 awarding 60% of Backwages to the Employee from the date of his termination reckoning the two 
decades of service he had under the management as a Peon on daily wage. As against that, the principle laid down 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a plethora of rulings aforementioned consistently hold that the Casual 
Employment terminates when the same is discontinued, and merely because a temporary or casual worker has been 
engaged beyond the period of his employment, he would not be entitled to be absorbed into regular service or made 
permanent, if the original appointment was not in terms of the process envisaged by the relevant rules. So the legal 
position settled at rest by the Hon’ble Supreme Court disentitles the I party to put forth any claim of reinstatement, 
regularization, continuity of service or back wages with consequential benefits. 
20. To sum up, the solitary materials viz., Ex W-| seires indicate the payment made to the I Party in the year 
205 alone for the month of March and November and there is no valid material proving that his engagement was 
continuous in nature and hhe performed duties under the II Party continuously till the date of his disengagement so 
as to show that his tenure of service at a time was more than 240 days in a calendar year and his disengagement was 
in violation of the provisions of Section 25F of the ID Act. So on legal principle and on factual matrix the I Party 
failed to establish a case on merit justifying the relief sought for in the instant Industrial Dispute. Eventually his 
Claim Petition fails and the same is liable to be dismissed. With this view Points No. | to 3 are answered 
accordingly. 
2. POINT NO. 4: In view of the above discussion, the I party is held as not entitled for any relief. 
22. In the result, the following Award is passed 
AWARD 
The Claim Petition is Dismissed. No order as to cost.

As per letter dated 02/][/205 by the Government of India, Ministry of Labour, New Delhi, the reference 
is made to this Tribunal under Section-l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (in short the ‘Act’)as per Notification 
No. L-260/28/20I5-(IR(M)) dt. 02/I/205. The dispute under reference relates to: 


5754 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA AUGUST 6, 2025/SHRAVANA 25, 947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“Whether the action of M/s Samanta & Company, Sub Contractor of M/s Heavy Engineering in 
removing Shri Girdhar and 467 other without giving notice and retrenchment benefit is justified? If so, 
what relief to Shri Girdhar and ॥67 others workmen entitled to?” 


According to the Workman Union, their Registration No. is 2764 and the Workman Girdhari with 67 others 
mentioned in the list attached are members of the Union. They have been regularly working since 2008 in the 
Overhandling Plant and Coal Handling Plant of Bhilai Steel Cement under the contracts. The HEC plant is the 
main contractor and M/s Samanta and Company is the sub-contractor. When the Workman Union raised the issue 
of none payment of wages of the Workman engaged by the sub-contractor M/s Samanta and Company, they 
illegally terminated these workman without any notice or compensation. The Union raised dispute in this respect 
which could not be conciliated, hence, reference was sent to this Tribunal by the appropriate Government. 


According to the Workmen Union, the termination of services of these workmen without notice or 
compensation and without approval of the Competent Authority is in violation of Section 25(F), 25(G), 25(H) 
and 25(N) of the Act. Hence, is unjust, illegal and arbitrary. These workmen have been continuously working 
since 2008 till the date of termination of their services by M/s Samanta & Company. The Workmen Union has 
requested that holding the action of Management illegal, these Workmen be held entitled to be reinstated with all 
back-wages and benefits. 


In their written statement of defense, filed by M/s Samanta & Company, they have taken a case that firstly, the 
dispute is not maintainable because the Workmen Union directly approached the Labour Commissioner before 
approaching the Management with respect to their grievances. It is further the case of contesting Management 
that, they were working on a project and execution of the workers allotted to them as contractors was dependant 
on fulfilling of drawing, site plant and raw material etc. there is continuity of work, hence, though the workmen 
might have worked in the projects in different spell of time but none of them worked continuously with the 
Management as claimed by them. The management further submitted that they have deposited the PF dues of 
these Workmen and have also denied that these Workmen were terminated from job. Rather they themselves left 
the job in different spell of time between 2009 to 20l4. Hence, according to Management, their action is not in 
violation of the Act. The Management has requested that the reference be answered against the Workmen Union. 


In evidence, the Workmen Union has filed a bunch of Photocopy documents, but they have been not proved it. 
None of the parties have produce any evidence in form of affidavit or proved documents. 


On the argument stage also, none was present from the side of Workmen Union, argument of Shri Rakesh 
Shrivastava Learned Counsel for Management of M/s Samanta & Company were heard. No written arguments 
have been field by any of the parties. I have gone through the record also. 


From perusal of record in the light of arguments, the reference itself is the issue for determination. 


It is the case of the Workmen Union, that they have worked continuously with Management of M/s Samanta 
and Company since 2008 till date of their disengagement and have completed more than 240 days in employment 
in every year including the year preceding the date of their disengagement. This allegation has been denied by 
Management. Hence, the burden to prove this fact of continuous employment is on the Workmen Union in which 
they have been failed, because they neither proved any document nor have examine any witness, hence holding 
the continuous engagement of the Workmen with the Management as alleged by Workmen Union not proved, it is 
held that, the action of termination of services of these Workmen is not in violation of the Act. 


In the light of above discussion and findings, the reference deserves to be answered against the Workmen 
Union and is answered accordingly. 


No order as to cost.
